facts.statement: Fossils of Nanosaurus have been found in the Morrison Formation of the south-western United States.
facts.quote: Its fossils are known from the Morrison Formation of the south-western United States.

facts.statement: The species Nanosaurus agilis was named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1877.
facts.quote: The type and only species, Nanosaurus agilis, was described and named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1877.

facts.statement: Modern research classifies Nanosaurus as a basal member of the Neornithischia clade.
facts.quote: Nanosaurus is today considered a basal member of Neornithischia.

facts.statement: Othniel Charles Marsh originally described Nanosaurus species as being fox-sized.
facts.quote: He regarded both species as small ("fox-sized") animals.

facts.statement: Specimens of Nanosaurus measured between 2 and 2.2 meters in length and weighed between 20 and 30 kilograms.
facts.quote: It was a small animal, with specimens previously assigned to Drinker and Othnielosaurus measuring 2 - 2.2 m long and weighing 20 - 30 kg.

facts.statement: Nanosaurus had short, broad hands with short fingers.
facts.quote: The hands were short and broad with short fingers.

facts.statement: Nanosaurus possessed small, leaf-shaped cheek teeth with ridges and denticles, while its premaxillary teeth were less ornamented.
facts.quote: It had small leaf-shaped cheek teeth (triangular and with small ridges and denticles lining the front and back edges), and premaxillary teeth with less ornamentation.

facts.statement: Nanosaurus had thin, cartilaginous intercostal plates running along its ribs, a trait shared with other neornithischians.
facts.quote: Like several other neornithischian dinosaurs, such as Hypsilophodon, Thescelosaurus, and Talenkauen, Nanosaurus had thin plates lying along the ribs. Called intercostal plates, these structures were cartilaginous in origin.

facts.statement: A 2025 study argued that the type specimens of Nanosaurus and related genera are too fragmentary to confirm they represent the same animal, suggesting they should remain as nomina dubia.
facts.quote: A 2025 study by Paul Barrett and Susannah Maidment failed to recognize autapomorphies (unique derived traits) or unique combinations of characters in the fragmentary or poorly preserved type specimens of Nanosaurus, Laosaurus, Othnielia, Othnielosaurus, and Drinker.

facts.statement: Some researchers tentatively suggest Drinker might be a Jurassic pachycephalosaur, which would make it the oldest known member of that group.
facts.quote: While this identification is highly tentative, it would make Drinker the only known Jurassic pachycephalosaur, and as such, the oldest member of the clade, filling a ghost lineage implied by the existence of Late Jurassic ceratopsians.

facts.statement: Nanosaurus was a very small dinosaur compared to the giant sauropods found in the same area.
facts.quote: Nanosaurus was one of the smaller members of the diverse Morrison Formation dinosaur fauna, diminutive in comparison to the giant sauropods.

facts.statement: Fossils of Nanosaurus have been found in stratigraphic zones 2 through 5 of the Morrison Formation.
facts.quote: Nanosaurus is present in stratigraphic zones 2-5.

facts.statement: While typically viewed as a small, fast herbivore, some researchers like Bakker in 1986 suggested Nanosaurus was an omnivore.
facts.quote: Typically, Nanosaurus has been interpreted like other hypsilophodonts as a small, swift herbivore, although Bakker (1986) interpreted Nanosaurus as an omnivore.

facts.statement: Nanosaurus belongs to the parent group Neornithischia.
Nanosaurus is classified within the dinosaur class Ornithischia.
There are 32 recorded fossil occurrences of Nanosaurus in the Paleobiology Database.
